summary: A mailing list of the ARPANET liaisons and others who should receive formal documents like RFCs by post in 1971. It names contact people at each site and replaces RFC 95. It was replaced by RFC 168.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone book for the people who need to get the newest papers by mail. Each site lists who to send them to.

subtitle: A contact list for distributing the early RFCs to ARPANET sites

tldr.problem: The ARPANET needed a way to deliver formal RFCs and documents to all the sites and liaisons working on the network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 155 lists the name, address and contact information for the person at each ARPANET site who should receive RFC documents by mail.
tldr.outcome: This was the first formal mailing list for RFC distribution. It was replaced by RFC 168 as the network grew.

facts.label: Delivery method
facts.value: Postal mail (air mail for distant sites)

today: RFC 155 is historic and obsoleted. It was replaced by RFC 168, which expanded the mailing list as the ARPANET grew. This early document is significant as the first formal RFC distribution list.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 155 is a mailing list published in May 1971. It lists the names and postal addresses of the people at each ARPANET site who should receive copies of RFCs and other formal network documents. This is the first official mailing list for RFC distribution.

The list covers primary liaisons at each major site (like UCLA, Stanford, MIT, and others), non-site contacts, and NIC Station Agents who help distribute documents locally.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone book of who to mail papers to at each computer site.

sections.title: The Network Sites
sections.content:
The list includes liaisons from about 20 primary network sites. Each site contributes to the ARPANET research and needs to receive the formal RFCs by postal mail. The sites include computing centers at universities (MIT, Stanford, Harvard, UCLA), research companies (RAND, BBN, SRI), and government agencies (ARPA).

In addition, the RFC identifies non-site organizations that need documents, such as IBM, and individual NIC Station Agents at each site who collect and distribute documents locally.
sections.plainLanguage: It lists computer centers at universities and research companies that worked on the network, plus the people who helped pass the papers around.

sections.title: Scope and Limitations
sections.content:
This list covers only those who should receive initial distribution of RFCs. The RFC notes that it supersedes RFC 95 and corresponds to the Current Directory of Network Participants. The list is specific to 1971 and reflects the structure of the ARPANET at that time.

The mailing arrangement assumes postal delivery via air mail for distant sites, which was necessary because email did not yet exist on the ARPANET.
sections.plainLanguage: This is just for 1971, when people sent papers by airplane mail. Email did not exist yet.
